utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Q, may we continue from where we left off yesterday? The last document we discussed was Z1963,8, and that was the form and declaration by the people who didn't wish to be exchanged. Can we go a step further? It is Z1963,9, that is the next document, and it is a list of individuals who did not wish to be exchanged. There were some 15 names on the list, including Peter Kuhta and Milka Kuhta, who are mentioned in this document. I am sure you remember the document; it was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that we don't have the statements of all these individuals? Only for Petar Kuhta do we have a signed statement saying that he did not wish to be exchanged; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, among these papers, we only have his statement tendered, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As we're talking about exchange, you became president of the commission in June, on the 1st of June, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And together with you in the commission was Kahric Nijaz, called Nidzo, and Jasmin Krnjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June, in the secondary school in Novi Travnik, there were 15 workers detained from the Bratstvo factory, they were the security detail there, and that was the first exchange that you took part in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was the first exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know about these 15 civilians who were exchanged on the 25th of June, 1993, with the mediation of your commission.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In July 1993, in the villages of Vodovod and Bukvica, 60 Croats were detained, 16 men, 29 women, and 15 children. Do you agree with that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with respect to the word "imprisoned," that is to say, they were in their homes. They were absolutely free in their homes, of course as much as the wartime circumstances allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but your side said to the HVO that 11 men were detained at the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July 1993, do you agree with me when I say that a total, that is to say, on the side held by the BH army, that there were 327 civilian Croats imprisoned, detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you there. I hear that figure for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the total number, the UNHCR made up a list of 183 civilian Croats who were detained in the village of Senkovici alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that. They were people who were living in their own homes, who tilled their own land, who lived with their families in their own homes, and as I said yesterday, most of those people did not wish to be exchanged, and that was the problem. It was a problem that the commission had to face, had to deal with, because when you go to see the people, the people say, "We don't want to be exchanged," and finally, they said, "All right. We can be exchanged but on condition that we don't have to go to the lower part of town of Travnik, but in the direction of Herzegovina or Croatia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you said that yesterday. So we don't agree with the term used "detained," or "imprisoned"; we agree with the number of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, I said in the exchange, all for all, that on the occasion, about 200 people, 200 individuals crossed into the part of town under the control of the HVO. These were people who lived in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood you. Thank you. As we mentioned the village of Senkovici, do you agree with me when I say that the representative of the HVO -- and first of all, I have in mind Dr. Zdenko Kranjc -- for the first time were in a position to visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Dr. Zdenko Kranjc was the first representative of the HVO who had occasion to visit the inhabitants of Senkovici in order to ascertain their health condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Zdenko Kranjc went with us to visit the Senkovici village and the inhabitants there to size up the situation, to see that the people were living normally there in their own village and to see for himself and to be told by them that they did not wish to be exchanged. Because, as I said, this was a great problem for me as president of the commission, how to convince the other side that people quite simply did not wish to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You've already said that. Let me finish asking my question, please. We're talking about the events that took place on the 19th of August, 1993, and that was when Dr. Kranjc visited the village, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact date, but I have it recorded somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the inhabitants of Senkovici on that occasion, in front of Dr. Kranjc, told you that they do wish to be exchanged and not that they do not wish to be exchanged, as you wanted to convince the HVO earlier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that visit very well. When we came to the village, they remained adamant at the beginning, but afterwards, Dr. Zdenko Kranjc asked a separate meeting with all of them, and I enabled him to have that meeting; I had nothing against it. After that second meeting, they changed their minds. So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When we're speaking about the inhabitants of Senkovici, they were forced to hold the front line both towards the Serbs and towards the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. No, it's not true. It's not true. If I may be permitted to say something, they were in a much better position than many Bosniaks who went up to the front line to fight. They were with their own families in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what I wanted to say was that they held the front line at Mravinjac, Kamenjas, towards the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict between the HVO and the army, there were lines which had both the members of the Armija and the HVO together jointly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted, when speaking about the documents that you looked at yesterday, to look at a document which is Z1963,12, and the document contains a total of 40 documents and they are all official notes, as we agreed yesterday; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, 22 of these 40 official notes are based on what we call operative data, which means that it does not state the source of the information. Is that not right? Let me give you an example to facilitate matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be the witness can agree with that without being taken to an example. Do you agree, Witness Q, that at least some of these are based on sources which aren't identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that. I think that this is just a small portion of the notes, official notes, and that there were many more in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if we agree in this matter, then we needn't go into those documents any more. We discussed them yesterday. Let me just round off what we mentioned yesterday in connection with the Stari Soliter building, and the Court has already heard about this. Tell us, please, Mr. Q, do you agree that across the road from this high-rise building was another high-rise which the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina held as a military facility? I think it is the high-rise which was partially burnt. Anyway, there was a fire in 1992 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a high-rise which the members of the HVO set fire to by shooting at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. So it is not a military facility, in fact, but was it held by the BH army in the period we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: After it was set fire to, it was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just indicating the testimony by Witness C, so I don't need to go into this matter with this particular witness. Your Honours, if I may now, I have just taken a look at my note, when Witness C, on the seventh day of our deliberations, the 20th of April, 1999, gave his testimony, he answered one of your questions, that is to say, "What was the condition set by the HVO to let the inhabitants of that high-rise leave?" I should like now, if I may, just to ask for some precision, that is to say, my own stand in that regard, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that occasion, I accepted what Witness C said, more or less, but I think that it is true that the HVO really did impose a condition and said that it would leave the tenants -- let the tenants go on condition that the Croats who were detained by the BH army side, and there they had in mind the village of Trenica and Senkovici, that those individuals should be exchanged for the inhabitants of the high-rise. So that is the precision that I would like to make in relation to the answer I gave you on that occasion. I said that on page 932 of the transcript. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking about the exchange, I omitted to ask you one thing. In the village of Opara, in the elementary school, there were 25 detainees, Croats, in the summer of 1993, in July 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not take part in their exchange, therefore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the villages, on the 2nd of June, Trenica, Bugojcici, Petocici, Potocani, Bistro, in those villages, 47 individuals were detained, 80 men, 24 women, and five children. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree in the wording you have used, "detained," that is to say, "imprisoned". We know what "imprisoned" means. As I say again, those people were in their own houses; they had water. They didn't have electricity, but they had water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that those people were never registered with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about seeing Mr. Kordic yesterday on several occasions on television. I think you'll agree that he was wearing a uniform on some occasions and civilian clothing on others.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear you say what period you were talking about when you said you saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him since my arrival in Bosnia; that is to say, from August onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean August 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you for those specific details because of the conclusions you drew on the basis of what Mr. Kordic had said, and you say that the same conclusions were repeated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of the speech, but that was the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't speak about one speech that he made but of several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I saw him on television on many occasions. He wasn't on television only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions to ask this witness with regard to what Mr. Kordic said, although the Defence does not agree with the conclusions that are made by the witness as to what Mr. Kordic had said when he appeared on television. So that is what we contest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, did you go about your business, as the representative and president of the commission for exchange, to the villages of Ruda, Pecine, and Margetic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained yesterday to the Prosecutor that you were never in the military police, as Commander Yorke said, who investigated the events in the village of Lazine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I said I was a member of the -- I was never a member of the BH army and, by the same token, a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I looked at Z1963.10, written in English. It is a statement, and he understood you both to be a military policeman and also an officer for the exchange of individuals in Bosnia-Hercegovina of the Novi Travnik Brigade, as an officer for exchange in this portion of the brigade and as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what Captain Yorke thought of that. I know that I worked at the time. I contacted him when it came to exchanges of this kind and pulling out the remains of -- the bodily remains at Begino Brdo, in the Begino Brdo area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of his report, Mr. Yorke says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Naumovski, the witness has said that he doesn't understand how Captain Yorke came to that conclusion. There seems little point going on about it. We've got the report, and if you want to comment on it, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted, so we've dealt with that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The essential point is that Mr. Yorke noted that you agreed to a ceasefire that had been agreed upon previously and that you told him about the events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday that you were not an eyewitness of the particular event, that is to say, when those people were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not, but every inhabitant of the upper part of town, or Kalinska Street, as we call it, remembered that event very well, and it was recounted afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, along with this report, in your papers we do not have the post-mortem findings. You said that a physician examined the bodies, but we have no findings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you thinking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the three -- that is to say, two bodies that were found in the period when Captain Yorke was there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attach a single post-mortem finding. This was just a report of mine to the Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But in your reports, we cannot see whether the injuries were injuries during the -- while the people were alive or whether the injuries were done to the body after death.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a pathologist. I didn't see the bodies. In the Sahinovic -- Muhamed Sahinovic case and Hajdar Mujic, I did talk to the coroner, the physician, who described in detail the state in which these people found themselves after the exchange, and you will notice in the report that I used different terms, terms of the medical profession, used by the medical profession. So they were direct eyewitnesses. Dr. Suvad Grizic was one of them, and the whole event was taped by Mirad Silajdzija. I'm talking about Sahinovic and Mujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to say, in general terms, that in what you wrote, there is no mention of whether the injuries were incurred during the individual's life or afterwards, after they had already died. Do we agree there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the report on the exchange that took place, and it was not a post-mortem report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't think we need tire the Court further with that matter. Your Honours, I beg your indulgence for just one moment. I think that I am drawing to a close. In fact, I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Q. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I'm a lawyer from Zagreb in this case, and I am the Defence counsel, with Mr. Kovacic, of the accused Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a number of questions, and I should like you to answer them to the best of your knowledge and recollection. Mr. Q, tell us, please, how long have you been a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 17 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, which police schools you attended, academies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen's secondary school in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Q, when you attended these secondary schools for policemen, did you study the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any provisions of the criminal code which refer to police matters within this code of criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, I can take it that you know the provision of Article 151 of the previous Law on Criminal Procedure, which speaks about official notes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know the stipulations of that provision, will you agree with me when I say that an official note is one of the ways in which the police documents individual events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that an official note is so-called informal evidence within the criminal procedure in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Q, what does the police do after it compiles an official note, as a rule? Does it then file a criminal report in its further investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: An official note is, in fact, the next step to take to ascertain the truth of a given matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a police investigation is conducted, then a criminal report is filed to the Prosecutor's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Q, that in cases of this kind, the ones that were tabled as evidence, whether any criminal reports were filed with regard to the looting of Bosniak citizens in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the police identified the perpetrators of the burglaries and looting that took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because they were wartime circumstances. It was a total blockade, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, in view of the fact that the perpetrators remained unidentified, to ascertain whether they were members of military units, or civilians, or if they were members of military units, which units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not possible at the time. It was not possible to ascertain that. But according to the insignia on their uniforms, they could have known, and as I said yesterday, it was frequently that these perpetrators were masked, that is to say, you couldn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I take your point. I looked through the official notes that were shown to you yesterday and that you have before you, and as a general concept, it says that the perpetrators were members of the HVO, but it is not said which unit. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's not mentioned, then it isn't, is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, a moment ago you said that they were in uniform and that they had HVO insignia. You also told us that from time to time, you wore a military uniform, although you were not a military man. Did you have any insignia on the uniform that you occasionally wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, no, I had none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "usually", does that mean that sometimes you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I did, as a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about a military uniform, sir, camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms were worn by policemen too; in war, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Q, do you know somebody nicknamed Sosa in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that that individual was a suspect for many crimes committed in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I do know that he was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think the Novi Travnik 308th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on now to another topic, Mr. Q. You said that you were a member from the 1st of June, 1993, and president of the exchange commission. Could you define for us the commission? Was it a civilian body or was it a military body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a body that was appointed by the war presidency of the municipality of Novi Travnik; that is to say, it was appointed by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would table reports to the war presidency as the civilian authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, would you please take a look at Exhibit 1963,7? Would you look at the lower right-hand corner of that document, which is where your signature is under number 2, and above it says, "The BH army commission". You signed the document. You told us that the commission was a civilian body. How, then, can you explain this particular fact on the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this record was drawn up by the commission for exchange of the Croatian Defence Council for Novi Travnik, and that's how they wrote it; although, if we take into account the circumstances under which the exchange took place, then this was practically up at the front line. So it was under exceptionally dangerous circumstances, and so you try and get the job done as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Q, despite the fact that you signed this record as a member of the commission of the BH army, you state that you were never a military man but a civilian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at page 2 of the record, which says "HVO commission." Were these individuals civilians or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean Josip Brodovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but according to the heading, I would say that they were members of the Croatian Defence Council. This is their document; they wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you've already told us that, Mr. Q. What do you mean when you say "the Croatian Defence Council," a civilian or military institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Q, do you know who, in October 1993, was in command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, in Novi Travnik, next to the old high-rise which we have talked about, there are at least four other tall apartment buildings, that is, the Koric, Novoteks, and the Novotekna, as their names are; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are high-rises. I don't know if they are the same height or one or two higher or lower, but they are all about ten stories high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that they are the dominant structures in town, that is, based on their height?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the height, yes. Perhaps there is -- they would be matched by Splicanka in the lower part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September of 1993, you said that the HVO had controlled the old high-rise building. Do you agree with me that this building was at the very line of separation of the two confronted parties in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the immediate vicinity of the line of separation, more closer to the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, who controlled the Koric high-rise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a single building by that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps your mind would be refreshed if you see a sketch.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Koric?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, my apologies. You're quite right. Could you now answer that question? Who controlled the Koric high-rise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was controlled by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was that building from the line of separation in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say with precision, some 70 metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's very close, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Q, let me take you back to 1991 and early 1992 for a moment. Is it true that young men from the Novi Travnik area at that time were going to the Republic of Croatia, which had been attacked by the JNA and the Serbian and Montenegrin paramilitary units, to fight for the Republic of Croatia against the attackers? Do you remember whether there were such young men who went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of a single case from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know anything about that, I have no further questions of you, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Q, the Defence has indicated on several occasions, in connection with this exchange between the residents of the Stari Soliter building and the Croats who were in the area under the control of the Bosnian army, that this was an exchange of prisoners. Let me ask you the question once again: The Croats who were in the area under the control of the Bosnian army, were they detained by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I have already said, it is inappropriate to compare people who were held in the Soliter as detainees and people who lived at peace in their own homes, with their families. They had their own livestock; they were spared going to the front lines. I cannot, under any circumstances, agree that these people were prisoners because, after all, those people didn't want to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those people could engage in their regular activities, to the extent that that was possible in times of war. They could tend their farms and engage in other normal activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so. One of the reasons why they didn't want to go down there was because they knew that all men of military age would immediately be engaged as HVO soldiers; whereas in their villages, they were left in peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence also spoke to you about a list of 123 Croatian prisoners established by the United Nations Commission for Refugees. Have you seen that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber, this list referred to a moment ago, that the Office of the Prosecutor is not aware of the list, and if the Defence has one, the Office of the Prosecutor would be glad to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A question has been addressed to you regarding the identification of the people who conducted acts of violence and evictions which were the subject of official reports drawn up by your service. On one of the documents that you yourself signed -- it is a document dated the 10th of June, 1993 -- it appears that one of the victims recognised among the perpetrators of these acts of violence a man called Zuti, Andro Androvic, known better under the name Zuti. This note is the one with the reference number Z1963,1 -- 1963,1 -- and you indicate in this report, in this note signed by you on the 10th of June, 1993, among them, Mr. Zaim Ramic, and you say that this person was beaten by HVO members, among whom he recognised Zarko Jandric also known as Zuti. Do you see this document? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about this person known as Zuti?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement by Zaim Ramic, living on Veljko Vlahovic Street, in Novi Travnik. I think there must be a mistake. His name was not "Jandric," but Andric, Zarko, known as Zuti, without the "J," therefore, whom I later had occasion to meet. In those days, I didn't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Andric, known as Zuti, came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he came from the village of Ricice, near Travnik or, rather, Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He came from Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just now, he's living in Nova Bila. As far as I know, he owns a cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that person was the head of a group known as "Zuti's Group," which was active throughout the conflict in the Lasva Valley in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. He is still active. Zuti still has a group of his own people who take care of him, as he is disabled. He was paralysed during a showdown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Zuti --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I don't really see that this arises from the cross-examination. We've heard now quite a lot about this individual and, no doubt, have a picture of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence complained that people could not be identified among the perpetrators. This is almost the only name that appears as one of the perpetrators. I will be finishing this point soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reference was made to someone called Susa a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he was a member of the BH army and of the 308th Brigade, that is what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sosa, yes. Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his real name Ivo Skocibusic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a misunderstanding. We are talking about two people with similar nicknames: One is Susa, he is Skocibusic, and Sosa is quite a different person who was on the side of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is precisely on this point I wish to hear your clarifications. A moment ago, the person you spoke of as a member of the 308th Brigade, was he Mr. Ivo Skocibusic, who was a leader of the HOS in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it was Sosa; Fikret Skopljak, I think his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness Q, thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness Q, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded and you are released. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Baggesen is back. Perhaps he can come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know what time we're sitting to today or how much of tomorrow we've got. My provisional plans are that Baggesen will be the last witness this week. I'm sure we can finish him this week, in what's left of today and tomorrow, but it seems that there would be very limited time available tomorrow and it wasn't possible to start another witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Some of us have a meeting at 5.00, so we'll have to finish at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. If he comes in, and Mr. Scott, who was taking him, will no doubt arrive imminently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I take it, we'll be able to finish this witness, if not today at least tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would hope today, Your Honour, but most certainly tomorrow. I think I should be through by a quarter to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it occurs to the Trial Chamber that it may be convenient tomorrow to deal with some of the legal points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It had occurred to me that we might deal with the issue about the expert witness, in particular. There's a substituted expert witness and there's opposition to that, and that certainly can be dealt with tomorrow. I've made arrangements for that material to be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I recollect the point. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a witness we propose to call called Ribicic, whose name couldn't be provided until recently. He's an expert in constitutional matters. There was an earlier expert in the same field named who had given evidence in the Blaskic case who, for various reasons associated with the problems of giving evidence here, was not able to give evidence live for this trial. Before the trial and aware of the difficulties that might develop, I had his evidence in the Blaskic case summarised and submitted to the Defence for possible agreement. They felt unable to agree and said that they would wish the witness for cross-examination, and presumably that's the same position that they would have taken had we made an application to have his transcript evidence read, and given that he's an important witness, there was every reason to believe that the application to cross-examine, even if we made an otherwise well-formed application to have his transcript evidence read, would be granted. Further, their Defence pre-trial brief dealt at great length with the issues dealt with in general by that witness and to be dealt with by Ribicic, and it's plainly an important part of their case. Indeed, it would appear that the pre-trial brief has been drafted, to this extent, by an expert they must have already retained. I can't believe that the matters spoken of are all within the knowledge and expertise of lawyers. So we set about finding an alternative expert, and maybe for similar reasons to those that were an impediment in the way of the first expert, we had some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is in now. We will get a copy of this material, will we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The material, the expert report, is not yet in form for service, but that's not in itself an impediment. Can I deal with it later on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Major, thank you for coming back. You are, of course, subject to the solemn declaration. If you'd like to take a seat, we will go on with your evidence this afternoon, and if it's not finished this afternoon, it will be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major. Sorry to force you to come back today, but we hope to be through with the questions that we have for you this afternoon. When we left, we had discussed the fighting that had occurred on the 16th of April, 1993, and I'd just like to draw your attention to the 18th of April, just a couple of days later. There's a special report on the Middle Bosnia situation, it's already been marked as Exhibit Z719, and I don't think I need to show you a copy unless you'd like to take a look at it, but it says that there is fighting going on throughout the whole of the area of responsibility of the BiH 3rd Corps, and this is on the 18th of April now, and the conclusion is that the worst fighting intensity for the time being is within the Vitez area, where both sides are using all available means against each other. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The same document refers to the situation in Zenica, where you were principally based, and it says: "The situation is quiet, as these lines are being typed, though throughout the night and the day, there was sporadic shelling." Would you agree that the shelling of Zenica was actually a rather routine event?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question on the problems with checkpoints. You said that the only issues that you ever encountered were -- any access issues were with HVO checkpoints, but isn't it true that you also encountered occasionally with ABiH checkpoints as well?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had, but not in the Lasva area, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a joint operation centre report dated the 22nd of April, 1993, which makes a reference to a team from the joint operations centre encountering a BiH checkpoint outside of the Klokoti gas factory. Just to orient you, that's somewhat to the northeast of Bilalovac. There, it says -- and it's northwest of Kiseljak. The joint operation centre report goes on to say that the BiH forces denied permission to the ECMM monitors to pass and threatened them with an RPG-7 and two M-60 machine guns. Was that an unusual event in your experience?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in the Lasva Valley area, essentially, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe that as south of the Lasva. That's why I gave you that other answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stand duly corrected. Thank you very much. Now, you were in Central Bosnia throughout the month of June 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the ABiH launched localised offensives against Croat pockets in Travnik, for example, and in Kakanj, as another example?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, you yourself noted in your diary that on June the 9th, as the fierce battles were raging around Kakanj, you actually saw ABiH forces using Croatian refugees as human shields to defend a power plant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the testimony about human shields that you gave, it's a very unfortunate observation, but it was really something that was going on fairly prevalently on both sides, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. You were asked some questions in connection with what you referred to as Croat propaganda, for lack of a better term, and two documents specifically, Z670 and Z696. The first one dealt with the matter of flags, and there are three names on the document. You identified this document as having Mr. Kordic's fingerprints all over it, but would it be fair to say that the document is not actually signed by him? I would be more than happy to show you a copy, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were not signed, only the names were mentioned in the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the point that I was making. I would like to have the usher show you Exhibit Z696, which is the second document that bears Mr. Kordic's name and about which you gave testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, just one real question about this document. You'll see that there are three separate names that appear on this document; right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you notice that the signature of each one there is by the same person?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who actually signed the document?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, turning to the testimony that you gave about atrocities against Croats in the days following the outbreak of fighting on the 16th, isn't it true that you visited several Croat villages to the west of Zenica on April the 20th and recorded, on page 8 of your diary, that you saw Croatian villages that had been burned down, many houses abandoned, and criminal gangs were running riot and pillaging houses?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the date again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's April the 20th, and it's on page 8 of the English version. I don't know whether that's of any help to you. That is, indeed, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next day, as I understand it, sir, you continued your tour -- actually, before I ask you that question, that's something that you saw and verified with your own eyes; correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same is true on April 22nd; you visited the village of Zalje, I believe --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Junhov and Fra Stipan Radic, and it's true that you knew that ten Croats had unfortunately been murdered in that village; correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that by Fra Stipan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw a 90-year-old man who had been shot and, unfortunately, a young girl, aged about three, who had been shot in the head in her bed?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that by Father Stipan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have no reason to disbelieve that, have you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In fact, you believe that you were being told the truth on that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The results of your investigation were ultimately incorporated into a report, a special report on Croats in Zenica, that was dated the 20th to the 21st of April, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the dates on my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's already been marked as an exhibit in this case, D25/1. You're more than welcome to take a look at it, but let me just draw your attention to a few things. Isn't it true that you found about four houses burned and 38 houses empty in the village of Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see the report to give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 25/1. That's it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, I do not want to consume too much time on this particular document, but this is one of the documents that you had a part in drafting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It, indeed, incorporated the results of your investigations and observations?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to go through all of these items of burned houses, robbings and so forth. The document speaks for itself and it's already in evidence. But wouldn't you agree there were in excess of 50 or so burned houses that you yourself saw, that there had been at least 14 Croats killed, and hundreds and hundreds of families had fled their houses as a result of this uncontrolled mayhem?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. The suggestion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The suggestion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- began as a result of HVO propaganda. The question is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat his intervention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat the point for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to Mr. Sayers' question for the reason that it's not consistent with the witness's testimony at all. The witness's testimony clearly on direct was that the movement by the Bosnian Croats out of the Cajdras area and the villages west of Zenica was as a result of HVO propaganda, not as a result of uncontrolled mayhem. The question is fundamentally misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think he's entitled to ask it in cross-examination. But so the witness can follow the point, I will rephrase it. Did they flee because of propaganda or was it because there was general uncontrolled mayhem, as it's put, going on around them? Major, do you have a view as to that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were only able to see the burned houses, and our conclusions were that the people there had left that area because it was not secure enough for them to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Major. Let me continue, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day that you described three buses, I think it was, were repossessed from you by HVO forces, to put it charitably, isn't it true that that occurred on April the 25th of 1993 and that that was the same day that five Croat civilians were massacred in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the buses were taken from us. I cannot recall what else happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I actually have the daily operations report from that day which I would like to have marked as an exhibit and which can be shown to you, and that may refresh your recollection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit is marked D86/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part of this document that I would like to draw your attention to specifically, Major, is paragraph C on the first page, which refers to the Croat village of Miletici and five inhabitants there having been murdered by shots and by knives. Everyone can read this document for themselves. Let me just ask you to inform the Trial Chamber of whether this is an accurate recitation of what you understand occurred in Miletici and what the ECMM understood occurred there.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I can see, one of our team was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Major Friis-Pedersen?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was together with Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need to go through this, Major. It really speaks for itself. Let me ask you to focus your attention on the next day. Do you remember visiting the village of Janjac, where about 50 per cent of the houses had been robbed, and an old woman had been killed by a sniper, and seven houses actually had been burned down by extremists with two soldiers in the basement, and they had burned to death as a result; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I make a report of that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you did. Let me have a copy of that marked. I think it's actually already been marked as Z832 in the Prosecution's direct examination. This is a report from Team Z1, which consisted of you and your colleague, Lieutenant Colonel Morsink, and the first numbered paragraph refers to your joint investigation into the events at Janjac. Wouldn't you agree that the report is precisely as I've just phrased it, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, do you know whether anything was done to investigate these terrible things on the part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember if there was a team put on Janjac, but that was a normal procedure when we saw things like that, that it was followed up by an investigation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- either by ECMM or UNPROFOR or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The things that we've gone over, as horrible as they are, really are not rumours. They are things that you yourself and your colleagues at the ECMM actually saw with your own eyes and verified as a result of your investigations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at Janjac as an isolated incident, it was not on rumour. But a lot of the other places we visited were -- there was nothing there to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. The things that I'm referring to, though, are the houses that had been burned down, the Croat houses, and you're not suggesting that the Croats burned those houses down themselves, are you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croats that had been shot to death or otherwise murdered, you're not suggesting that the Croats were responsible for murdering their own people, are you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Things like that happened on both sides, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question in this area, sir, and I think we can depart it swiftly. It concerns an event that occurred on June the 10th of 1993, when a shell was fired from Stari Vitez and exploded in a children's playground, literally blowing apart about eight children there, and that event was filmed by the BBC. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the name of the area?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the shell fell close to Gacice. If you do, you do know about it, and if you don't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: June the 10th, 1993, approximately between 6.00 and 8.00 in the evening, I believe.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in that area. I was operating in the Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Around that time, June the 10th, there was an ABiH offensive actually under way in Kakanj, which resulted in the expulsion of about 15.000 Croat refugees from the town, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why I was in the Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Let me turn to another subject that you covered in your direction examination, the fighting in Kiseljak. The Kiseljak municipality was actually part of Canton 7 under the Vance-Owen Plan; isn't that right? That was going to be a Muslim-controlled canton, I believe.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tried initially to gain access to the village of Gomionica, and you were stopped by one very old man with a very old rifle, I believe.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at one of the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the other checkpoint, you were stopped by troops who instructed you that they had received orders from Mr. Ivica Rajic not to permit you to pass; correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was the power in Kiseljak, so to speak, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two documents, one which you probably have not seen before but is useful by way of background, and one which I believe you may have seen before. The first is a document that I -- dated the 19th of April, 1993, that I would like to have marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D87/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. While you're looking at this document, if I could just have the usher mark the next exhibit, please, I'm showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D88/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Major, have you ever heard of a special forces unit of the ABiH known as the Black Swans?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document, D87/1, it looks like an order from Colonel Blaskic to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, and the fourth point in that order informs the Ban Jelacic Brigade that in Colonel Blaskic's estimation, an effort would be made by this special-purpose unit, the Black Swans, to try to infiltrate the ranks of the HVO in Kiseljak. You've never seen this document before, I take it, sir.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that when you went to Gomionica, you found, with one exception, no dead bodies of civilians?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, when you actually went to Gomionica, if you take a look at the next exhibit, there's a reference on page 2, under item 5, to the fact that no bodies were found, "except for one dead soldier from the Muslim fraction," it says, but I take it that it means "faction," "called Black Swan." Is it fair to say that you actually saw this dead soldier, since you were one of the authors of this report?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This soldier, he was not found in Gomionica. I cannot recall where he was found, but he was not in Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it says that he was found in Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. It would be fair to say that you found actually no bodies at all in Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But one of the special forces units was found in one of the villages to the northwest of Kiseljak on the 24th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, we don't know. He was an old man, what you call, in this special unit. We were able to identify him because of his, what are you calling it, on his shoulder --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insignia on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on his shoulder. But as far as I can recall, he was an old man. It could be someone put in the uniform. Just because you are finding a dead body in a uniform, it's not guaranteed that he belongs to that force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you, Major, that that's one possibility, but that's speculation, that he was put into the uniform. We simply have no way of determining that fact, do we?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found a man in a uniform who belongs to the Black Swans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Turning to June the 22nd, which is drawing towards the end of your tour through Central Bosnia, isn't it true that there was a rocket attack on the town of Kiseljak, with the Croatian part of the town hit by many rockets, resulting in the deaths of several children and the wounding of several others?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was actually in Vitez, but in the translation from my Danish diary to maybe the Croatian or the English, there's been some error. This attack was in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, the Croatian part of Vitez was hit by rockets --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and people were killed on the 22nd. All right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It said in the diary that I was together there with Pero Skopljak. It was not Pero Skopljak. It was another man. I made a mistake in my diary. It was not Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's no problem, sir, but --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the attack was in the Croat part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, the rockets landed in the Croat part, and Croats were killed as a result of the explosions.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Turning to one more subject, the testimony that you gave regarding the village of Rotilj. According to the special report that was marked as Z818, the ECMM concludes that the village was not defended by any BiH force. Are you sure that that's the fact, or isn't it true that the village was actually defended?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the team who went in, which was in the first days. I don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever discuss with Colonel Morsink the results of his findings regarding Rotilj and the conversation that he had with the local HVO commander about what happened in that village?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say then, sir, that you yourself actually do not know what happened in Rotilj and that you would defer factually to those who actually have more personal knowledge about the facts of that event than you do?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was not in Rotilj just after the incident, but a few days after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you don't recall having any conversations with Colonel Morsink about that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I was there together with him, but I cannot remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. With the Trial Chamber's indulgence, Colonel Morsink testified in the Blaskic case on page 10024 as follows, the question was: Q Tell us if you agree with your prior statement on page 7 when you said that you discussed this ... and he refers to Rotilj. ... with the local HVO commander and he said, he claimed that villagers had opened fire on his troops from a Muslim house and that one HVO soldier had been killed. Fighting had started and that was when the Muslims had been killed and seven Muslim houses were burnt. The Muslims had handed over 20 weapons and the young men taken to prison. I think this story was accurate. And the question was asked of Colonel Morsink: Q Is that a correct statement? A That's a statement I made in my special report, yes. Q And do you believe it to be true? And the response to that was: A I believe it to be true. Isn't that essentially what Colonel Morsink told you as well when you discussed the events of Rotilj with him?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked me if there was any defence in that area, I was thinking of BiH troops, but there were no BiH troops. I could not remember if there were inhabitants who tried to defend their own houses or not, but the people killed in Rotilj were not people who were trying to defend. I can remember there was a woman who was raped. I don't think she was raped because she tried to defend her home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to that woman?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion about what happened to her is really based upon what you were told by other people; right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the subject of gaols and prisoners, just a few questions on this topic. You actually visited, on April the 30th, 1993, a detention facility in Kiseljak where you found 48 civilian prisoners, all of whom were male and all of whom had been treated well; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then you visited the main military prison in Zenica on the 20th of April, ten days earlier, and the conditions that you found there were -- at least they're described in the English version of your diary -- worse than a hen house. Is that an accurate translation of what you recorded in your diary on page 7?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned that the conditions there were bad, they were not that bad, but I referred not to a hen house but another thing that the person who translated it could not understand, because it's a special Danish word or joke on it. This was in a small room, but not that small, and actually when I visited the different prisons down there, I often mentioned that it seems to be okay. When I say everything was -- the prisoners were treated fair, they had bread and water and they were allowed to have fresh air. It was not the Hotel Hilton, but they were allowed to have something to eat and something to drink and allowed to smoke cigarettes and have fresh air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I mean, just to put an end to this particular area, there were detentions of large numbers of civilians on both sides, and would it be fair to say that although the conditions were not, as you put it, the Hotel Hilton, they were not outrageously bad or particularly bad, in your view?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony with respect to communications. Let me just ask you, isn't it a completely normal tactic in wartime to try to cut the communication lines of the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between the forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that you only ever saw one large radio antenna in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing radio antennas in Vitez and other places, but I cannot recall the different places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the subject of the Zenica shelling of April the 19th, you've agreed that the shelling of Zenica was fairly regular both before and after April the 19th, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can recall, April the 19th was the first attack with artillery against Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after that, it became on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no question in your mind that the Serb artillery positions due west of Zenica at Pajinik [phoen] and just six kilometres northwest of Travnik, they had the range to hit Zenica, did they not?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. On the later attack, they shelled Zenica and they shelled the Croats in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the month of April, the Bosnian Serb artillery in the Travnik area was shelling not only Zenica, but also Vitez too?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to keep the kettle boiling, we think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that 130 people were actually seriously wounded in a shelling incident on the 21st of April, 1993, and that numerous uncounted people were killed in that shelling incident too.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, your diary is in evidence. As I see it, there was another shelling incident on May the 8th which you investigated.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What dates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May the 8th.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May the 8th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that resulted in your production of actually a written report regarding that item, that incident; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was no written report that you prepared regarding the April the 19th shelling incident, was there?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In fact, there's no reference in your diary on April the 19th of having made any kind of crater analysis or contemporary expert investigation of the provenance of the shells, is there?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the diary, because the diary was not meant for this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any artillery expertise beyond the training you received during basic training, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been commanding units with artillery, I have fired artillery myself --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twice? Did you say "twice"?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, myself. So I have a lot of work with artillery, but I'm not from the artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe yourself as an artillery expert or not?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's no question, though, that contemporaneously in your diary, you recorded that the shells were fired at 9.30 a.m., isn't that right, if you turn to the April the 19th entry?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's true that Zenica had actually many military headquarters; not only was it the headquarters of the 3rd Corps, but also the 7th Muslim Brigade had a headquarters there, as did the 314th Motorised Brigade, and the military police, and also the 301st Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew the model of howitzer that was used in this shelling incident, and did I hear you say that you believed it to have been a D30 model, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The maximum range of a D30-J is approximately 17,300 metres, as we covered. Is that consistent with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's able to have a longer range than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You would concede that what you did in terms of a crater analysis does not qualify as an exact science; wouldn't you agree with that, Major?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you are looking at this impact, it's actually very easy to see the direction from where the shell had been fired, and when looking on the splash marks and looking if you can find any of the shrapnel, it should be easy to see the size of the weapon that was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you perform any calculations or consult any authoritative works regarding ballistics to arrive at your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not do that in the ECMM because we were not assigned a military unit, but as far as I can recall, some of the UNPROFOR units were asked to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically, what you did was take a compass and point it at what you considered to be the centre line of the crater; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we did that from three out of six craters, and we found that they came from the same direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have the assistance of the representatives of the 3rd Corps in performing your investigation, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me have that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were, in fact, representatives of the 3rd Corps present as you were performing your observations of the craters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall if they were there on April the 19th, but often when we were visiting an area where we were doing some investigations in the BiH-held area, we had representatives from BiH and some of their experts, and we did the same when we were going to investigate impacts on HVO areas; then there were representatives from the HVO with us as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that with the exception of the April the 19th incident, your view was that every other incident in which artillery was used to shoot shells into Zenica, your view was that it was the Bosnian Serb artillery that was responsible for that damage?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
