utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, because its view claimed that the BiH were shelling the Vitez area, and BiH were claiming that the HVO were shelling Zenica. Therefore, it was important for us to find out who was responsible for the shellings, and if we couldn't tell the HVO and the BiH that it was the Bosnian Serb army that was shelling both of them, it would ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to agree with me that at 17.300 metres, a ten-degree error, if you made an error, would result in a deviation of 3.200 metres regarding your analysis of the point of origin of the shelling; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How much did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thirty-two hundred metres. You would not agree with that? That's fine. Do you know what the top of the -- or how high the shell travelled, sir, how far above the ground?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the maximum elevation point, if you'd like, the apogee of the ballistic was actually 6.000 metres for a D30-J, 122-millimetre howitzer?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall all the different weapons, but if you've looked it up --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the meteorological conditions were on that day?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that if you had, for example, 12.000-metre winds at 6.000 feet, that would result in a 500-metre deviation from a no-wind condition?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO actually had any meteorological facilities?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the way we saw the use of artillery in Bosnia, it didn't seem to us that they were experts in using those weapons --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we didn't see any military target hit by artillery. We only saw civilian areas hit by artillery. If there had been any artillery of soldiers who were able to guide the fire against the targets, then they would have had hit the targets, but it seems to us that they were just shelling just to shell an area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that just a few days after you performed the -- well, actually let me ask you one other question. You simply do not know what the target was on April the 19th by whoever was firing that artillery, whatever calibre it was, and wherever it was fired from, do you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that just a few days later, the ECMM actually recommended the installation of artillery-locating radar in the Zenica area to verify which units were firing and their targets so that there would be no question as to who was firing upon whom?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's information, I don't think there's any need for the witness to look at this; I'd just like to mark the daily operational report containing that recommendation as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you are drawing to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I had hoped that I'd be through by now, but I think I have about five more minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See how you get on towards a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you want me to continue or take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D89/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's information, the item that I read was on page 2, under paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other document I would just like to show you, Major, is the daily report that I believe that you and a colleague of yours prepared regarding the May the 8th shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D90/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just showing you document D90/1, Major. That is a copy of the report that you actually prepared regarding the shelling incident that occurred on May the 8th; correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions in connection with the order signed by Colonel Blaskic. Isn't it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going on to another topic, it may be more convenient to deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got about five minutes, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Five minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my best estimation, probably something more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will sit tomorrow. Yes, we'll sit at 2.30 tomorrow, and I hope we shall be able -- we must get through the witness, and also it would be convenient to have the legal argument too, so everybody should be prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Until what time is the Court thinking of sitting tomorrow? I have decided, I think, not to call another witness, but if there was going to be a substantial amount of the afternoon, it's just possible I could reorganise a witness and start one who could come back in many weeks' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We shall have to adjourn at 4.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, I'll take the decision and I'll not call another witness tomorrow. He will be part heard, in any event. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
